Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Seychelles Civil Status has regional offices on islands like Praslin serving rural populations. WHO SCORE assessment (2013-2018 data) states: "All data are exchanged electronically from local to regional offices and then to central offices: Paper-based locally, electronic processing". Birth registration requires in-person submission of paper maternity certificate at regional offices. Recent 2024 launches (SeyID virtual IDs, CertExpress online certificates) enable digital access to records but data entry remains by central officers on paper inputs. No evidence of digital recording at rural points; fits predominantly paper with central digitization (score 2). Completeness 90%.

revision_notes: The cited WHO SCORE PDF (who_score_syc_en.pdf) was fetched in full and does not contain the quoted text about civil registration data being 'exchanged electronically from local to regional offices'; it is a general health-data-systems assessment (surveys, SDG indicators, birth/death registration completeness scoring) with no such passage on civil registry office processes. That quote could not be verified and should not be relied upon. The department's own website confirms birth registration requires in-person attendance at one of three Civil Status offices (Victoria, Praslin, La Digue) with a paper maternity certificate; the 2024 SeyID and CertExpress launches digitise virtual ID issuance and certificate retrieval/ordering, not the underlying capture of vital events at the registration counter. Per the variable's guidance that only facility-level capture counts (not downstream digitisation), the original Value Code of 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed; the Comments' internal reasoning toward a score of 2 is not supported by the evidence found.
revised_comments: Civil registration in Seychelles is conducted in person at one of three Civil Status offices (Victoria, Grand Anse Praslin and La Digue), all under the Department of Immigration and Civil Status. Registering a birth requires attendance within 30 days with a paper maternity certificate and identity documents produced at the counter; there is no remote or online channel for the underlying registration event itself. The department's 2024 digital initiatives, SeyID (virtual identity cards) and CertExpress (online ordering of birth, marriage and death certificates), digitise the retrieval and issuance of documents rather than the initial capture of vital events. Data capture at the point of service therefore remains an entirely paper-based process, with any digitisation occurring centrally once records are consolidated into the National Population Database.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Seychelles (e.g., Praslin, La Digue, Mont Fleuri) record criminal cases and complaints using a national digital case management system built on FileMaker platform, funded by UNODC and developed by Transmedia. Deployed across all stations, which are connected nationwide, allowing point-of-service entry of incident reports, occurrence books, and case details on desktops/iPads. It replaced parallel manual records, digitizes intake forms, enables searches across districts, cross-references (vehicles, phones), and supports court use. Detective from Mont Fleuri station (Mahe rural-ish) confirms: "all police stations are connected... transformed the life of the Seychelles police force." Evolutions include 2023 Cautions module, digitized Occurrence Book. Some paper may linger for minor/admin tasks, but digital is standard at rural point-of-service. No evidence of majority paper or pilots only. Barriers: small population (98k), remote islands may limit infra/maintenance, but connectivity confirmed. National e-gov push aligns with rural reality.Winsoft International; Seychelles Police; Forensic Science Int.

revision_notes: Original Value Code of 3 (Mostly digital - some paper) is confirmed. The Winsoft International case study and the Seychelles Police directory verify that a FileMaker-based case management system is deployed across all police stations, including the Praslin and La Digue district stations, digitising incident intake, case tracking and cross-referencing since initial deployment, and evolving further with a Cautions module and ongoing digitisation of the paper Occurrence Book. Because the Occurrence Book digitisation is described as an ongoing modernisation rather than a completed transition, and no source confirms elimination of all paper processes (e.g. handwritten witness statements), there is no basis to promote this to 'Entirely digital' (4).
revised_comments: Seychelles Police operates a nationwide digital case management system built on the FileMaker platform (developed by UK-based Transmedia, originally funded via UNODC), deployed across all police stations including the district stations on Praslin and La Digue as well as those on Mahé. The system digitises intake forms for incident reports, supports case tracking, cross-referencing of vehicle registrations and phone numbers, and searches across districts, having replaced an earlier parallel manual record-keeping system. Recent enhancements include a Cautions module for minor offences and an ongoing project to digitise the Occurrence Book, previously a paper daily incident log. Some manual documentation likely persists alongside the digital system, for example handwritten statements taken at first point of contact, consistent with a predominantly digital but not fully paperless environment at rural stations.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Seychelles Ministry of Education operates a national EMIS for collecting school data on students, staff, infrastructure from all institutions, including primary schools on outer islands (rural equivalents). In 2019, AU's IPED piloted DataPlat digital platform at schools (e.g., Anse Royale secondary) to address prior issues of inconsistent, unreliable, slow paper-based collection methods, enabling direct digital entry to national repository. OpenEMIS advisors assisted MoE in 2025 ("jump-start" EMIS), indicating ongoing digital rollout. Annual Education Statistics booklets (2020-2024) published by EMIS section. No evidence of paper-only at schools post-pilots; small nation-wide system suggests predominant digital recording at rural primary schools for attendance/enrollment/grades/admin, score 3.

revision_notes: Original Value Code of 3 (Mostly digital - some paper) is revised down to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital). Community Systems Foundation's OpenEMIS Country Highlights 2025 states that Seychelles only 'joined the OpenEMIS community' in 2025, with training 'underway ahead of January 2026 rollout' — i.e. a school-level digital data-capture system was not yet in place at the most recent point for which evidence exists, and the country was still onboarding rather than operating a mature digital EMIS. This indicates the 2019 AU DataPlat pilot referenced in the Comments did not evolve into a sustained digital data-capture system used across schools; the Ministry's own account of that pilot describes the prior methods it was meant to replace as 'inconsistent, unreliable, slow' and 'paper-based'. A separate UAE-partnered Digital School Initiative launched in April 2026 targets classroom technology and teaching rather than administrative data capture. Taken together, the evidence points to school-level data capture (attendance, enrolment, grades) at rural primary schools remaining predominantly paper-based, with digitisation concentrated at the point of national aggregation (the annual Education Statistics compilation) rather than at the school itself.
revised_comments: Administrative data capture in Seychelles' primary schools, including those on the outer islands, has relied substantially on manual, paper-based collection feeding into the Ministry of Education's annual Education Statistics compilation. A 2019 pilot of the African Union's DataPlat platform, tested at Anse Royale, aimed to address inconsistent, unreliable and slow paper-based data collection, but did not become the Ministry's standing operational system. As of 2025 the Ministry has joined the OpenEMIS community and is undergoing training ahead of a planned January 2026 nationwide rollout of school-level digital data capture, alongside a separate UAE-partnered Digital School Initiative focused on classroom technology. School-level administrative records at rural primary schools therefore remain predominantly paper-based, with digitisation concentrated at the point of national data aggregation rather than at the school itself.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Seychelles (termed community health centres or PHCs on outer islands/districts) continue to rely predominantly on paper-based patient data recording, despite national eHIS rollout. The Ministry of Health's 2022-2026 Strategic Plan states data capture is "primarily paper-based" with duplicative tools, and eHIS implementation (started 2020) has stalled, creating an urgent need for transition Seychelles MoH Strategic Plan. The 2023 Annual Performance Report shows progress with 88% eHIS patient registration coverage in PHCs (up from 29% in 2022), but actual consultation recording lags, remaining below expectations even after EMR training for 140 doctors MoH Performance Report 2023. No specific rural/outer island distinctions, but given small scale (17 CHCs nationwide), rollout likely covers them. Digital systems like eHIS integrate surveillance/labs centrally, but point-of-care is hybrid. Barriers: stalled implementation, staff training/satisfaction, data quality. National ambition for full eHIS contrasts with persistent paper dominance at clinics Commonwealth WHO Assessment. Score 3 reflects majority digital registration standardizing, with paper fallback for consultations.

revision_notes: Original Value Code of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) is confirmed; the Comments' concluding line referring to a 'Score 3' is not supported by the evidence found and is not carried forward. The Ministry of Health's National Health Strategic Plan 2022-2026 and the Annual Health-Sector Performance Report 2023 (published July 2024) both confirm that data capture in clinics is 'primarily paper-based' and that the electronic Health Information System (eHIS), begun in 2020, had stalled and required a 'full continued roll-out' as a stated priority for 2024 - i.e. rollout remained incomplete going into 2024. A July 2025 Health Information Exchange Maturity Assessment workshop, run with Africa CDC support, further indicates the digital health system was still being assessed and matured rather than fully operational at point of care. This is consistent with the original score and does not support a promotion to 'Mostly digital' (3) or higher.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics and community health centres in Seychelles continue to rely predominantly on paper-based data capture. The Ministry of Health's National Health Strategic Plan 2022-2026 states that data capture is 'primarily paper-based', using a variety of duplicative reporting tools, and that implementation of an electronic Health Information System (eHIS), begun in 2020, stalled before requiring renewed effort. The Annual Health-Sector Performance Report 2023 (published July 2024) lists the 'full continued roll-out of digital health information systems' among the Ministry's priorities for 2024, indicating the rollout remained incomplete at that point, and a Health Information Exchange Maturity Assessment workshop held in July 2025 with Africa CDC support further indicates the system was still being matured rather than fully deployed. Point-of-care data entry at clinics is therefore best characterised as predominantly paper-based with a partial and growing digital component.
